newsitem.title: USA: U.S. investigators probe Maine tanker accident.
newsitem.headline: U.S. investigators probe Maine tanker accident.

text.p: Federal transportation safety officials launched an investigation on Saturday to determine what caused an oil tanker to strike a drawbridge, spilling more than 4,000 barrels (170,000 gallons/640,000 litres ) of fuel into Portland harbor.

The accident created both environmental and transportation problems, forcing officials to ban lobstering in a large area around the harbor and leaving a major commuter route to Maine's largest city unusable.

The 560-foot (170-metre) Julie N was entering Portland Harbor on Friday with a cargo of approximately 210,000 barrels of No. 2 distillate fuel when it struck a granite abutment on a bridge across the harbor, officials said.

The accident punched two holes in the ship's port bow. The 6-foot by 1-foot (two-metre by 0.3-metre) gashes allowed 2,100 barrels of the load and 1,950 barrels of bunker fuel used for the ship's engines to escape, officials said in a revised estimate on Saturday.

Coast Guard and National Transportation Safety Board officials declined on Saturday to speculate on a cause of the accident, which was the worst at this busy harbor in two decades. The investigation would take at least 10 days, they said.
The passage through the 80-year-old bridge is only 95 feet (28 metres) wide and well known in the maritime industry for its difficulty. The Julie N was 85 feet (25 metres) wide.

"All of a sudden there was a loud thunderous noise," said Bill Jewell, who happened to be taking a picture of the bridge the moment the ship hit. Jewell's photo showed a cloud of powdery debris flying from the area of impact.

Officials said quick response by emergency crews should reduce the environmental impact of the spill, but lobstering, fishing and shellfish harvesting was temporarily banned in the southern half of Casco Bay.
"The closure for shellfish could be long-term," warned Joseph Fessenden, director of the Maine Marine Patrol.

The harbor, which is a major port of call for both fishing boats and oil tankers, remained closed for cleanup operations. Oil collection equipment skimmed the water and containment booms surrounded the now-docked tanker.

State officials are also scrambling to fix the bridge, which is used by 33,000 drivers daily. A larger bridge is scheduled for completion next summer, but Gov. Angus King said he had been assured federal emergency funds would be available to repair the old structure.
The Liberian-registered Julie N is owned by New York-based Maritime Overseas Corp, a unit of Overseas Shipholding Group Inc. a company official said. It was chartered by Global Petroleum Corp.
